newsitem.title: FRANCE: French politicians flounder over far right.
newsitem.headline: French politicians flounder over far right.

text.p: French calls to ban the far-right National Front fell flat on Sunday, with party leader Jean-Marie Le Pen revelling in denunciations of his public declaration that races are unequal.
"You don't ban the plague, you fight it," Francois Leotard, head of the Union for French Democracy group, the junior partner in the ruling centre-right coalition, said in allusion to Le Pen.

Mainsteam politicians have savaged Le Pen for saying racial differences are a "fact". But almost all shied away from proposals to ban his party, fearing a backlash of sympathy for his anti-immigrant views.

"France, cradle of human rights, is the world's only nation where a politician...can make racist statements, wallow in them and get a greater audience, instead of a trial or a ban," the Journal du Dimanche newspaper said in an editorial on Sunday.

Le Pen, who won 15 percent of the vote in 1995 presidential elections but whose party has no seats in parliament, has repeatedly hijacked national political debate towards his far-right agenda on race, immigration or jobs.
He wants to expel three million immigrants.

"Every day the facts show us that races are different," he said on Saturday, when he led a racially charged march through the Mediterranean port of Marseille to denounce the death of a white teenager alleged to have been killed by an Arab youth.
On Sunday night, he quoted from the works of Leon Blum, a respected pre-war Socialist prime minister and from 19th century politician Jules Ferry talking about racial inequality.
"They would be in jail today if they said that," he commented. He admitted that he called Saturday's march because of the racial origins of the crime.

Le Pen, a wily 68-year-old whose popularity feeds on controversy and fears about high unemployment, has said French civilisation is superior but has stopped short of naming any supposedly "inferior" races.
Justice Minister Jacques Toubon reiterated on Sunday that he wanted to stiffen anti-racism laws, saying that Le Pen's race remarks were too vague to be punished by existing legislation.
"We need a law that makes it possible to punish indirect provocation, indirect calls for racist acts, hatred, violence or discrimination based on race," he said in a television interview.
He said he wanted to double sanctions for racist crimes and to speed up court trials of racists. He said he hoped a draft bill would be ready for parliament next month.
Toubon and most other mainstream politicians have rejected calls to ban the National Front, floated by former Socialist leader Henri Emmanuelli.
Successive governments have hoped to defuse the Front's lure by eradicating unemployment, but the latest dispute has revealed the emptiness of their arsenal.

Opinion polls indicate that Prime Minister Alain Juppe is unpopular with voters, perceived as out of touch with job worries and placing too much emphasis on economic austerity in order to qualify for a single European currency from 1999.
